# Tokens and brands

> Three tiers, alias chains, and the override-only rule that lets one stylesheet serve every brand.

This is the chapter that matters. If you understand the three tiers, alias chains, and the
override-only rule, everything else in girih is a detail. All the values on this page are real —
extracted by running girih's own engine over `examples/acme-ds`.

## What a token is, exactly

A token is a named design decision written in DTCG JSON. Two keys carry the weight:
`$value` and `$type`.

**tokens/global.tokens.json (excerpt)  [You write this]**

```json
{
  "radius": {
    "$type": "dimension",
    "sm":   { "$value": "4px" },
    "md":   { "$value": "8px" },
    "lg":   { "$value": "16px" },
    "pill": { "$value": "999px" }
  }
}
```

Note that `$type` is declared once on the group and inherited by every member.
`radius.md` is a dimension without saying so itself. girih flattens this into a map
keyed by dotted path, and that flat map is what every later stage speaks:

**after mergeTokenFiles()  [girih writes this]**

```
radius.sm    tier=global  type=dimension  value="4px"
radius.md    tier=global  type=dimension  value="8px"
radius.lg    tier=global  type=dimension  value="16px"
radius.pill  tier=global  type=dimension  value="999px"
```

> **🟢 In plain words**
>
> A token is a variable for a design decision. `radius.md` means "our medium corner
> radius" — and the point of the name is that the _meaning_ stays put while the
> _number_ is free to change. Anything that wants a medium corner asks for the name, so one
> edit moves everything.

## Why three tiers

girih requires tokens to live in one of three tiers. The tier is inferred from the filename —
`global*.tokens.json`, `semantic*.tokens.json`, and anything under
`tokens/components/` — and a file girih cannot classify gets a
`GIRIH2004` warning and is treated as semantic.

| Tier | Holds | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Component** | 54 tokens in the example | `button.radius`, `button.primary.background`, `input.border-focus`, `dialog.backdrop` |
| **Semantic** | 25 tokens | `radius.control`, `color.primary`, `color.on-primary`, `typography.size-md` |
| **Global** | 31 tokens | `radius.md = 8px`, `color.blue.600 = #2563EB`, `space.4 = 16px` |

_References flow downward only: component → semantic → global._

Each tier answers a different question, and the questions are asked by different people:

| Tier | Answers | Example | Who changes it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Global** | What values exist in our palette at all? | `color.blue.600 = #2563EB` | Rarely — this is the raw material |
| **Semantic** | What does this value _mean_ to us? | `color.primary = {color.blue.600}` | Design leads; brands override here most |
| **Component** | What does _this component_ use? | `button.primary.background = {color.primary}` | Whoever owns the component |

> **🔵 Rule — The tier rule**
>
> A reference may point at its own tier or a lower one. Never upward. Component may reference
> semantic and global; semantic may reference global; global references nothing. Violations are a
> build error, reported by `validateTierDirection()`.
>
> Without this rule the tiers are just folders. With it, you can reason about blast radius: a
> global change may affect anything, a component change affects that component. That guarantee is
> the whole return on the extra indirection.

<details>
<summary><b>Why not two tiers? Or four? — the argument for exactly three</b></summary>

**Two tiers** (raw + component) means every component references raw values directly. Change
"our primary blue" and you must edit every component that used the blue — and you must know
which uses of `blue.600` meant "primary" versus "that particular blue". The
information about _why_ a value was chosen is nowhere.

**Four or more tiers** is where teams usually end up by accretion, and the cost is that
nobody can predict where a value comes from. Each hop is a place to look during debugging. The
example workspace's longest chain is three hops, which is already enough that the
[walker widget below](#walker) earns its keep.

**Three** is the smallest number that separates the three questions in the table above:
what exists, what it means, what uses it. That separation is what makes a brand overlay a
values-only operation.

</details>

## Alias chains

A token whose `$value` is `{another.token}` is an alias. Chains form
naturally from the tier structure. Here is the real chain for a button's corner radius on the
default brand:

| Tier | Token | Resolves to | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `component` | button.radius = {radius.control} | `8px` |  |
| `semantic` | radius.control = {radius.md} | `8px` |  |
| `global` | radius.md = 8px | `8px` |  |

Three hops, three tiers, and only the last one holds an actual number. Now the same chain on the
`seller` brand — same structure, one overridden value:

| Tier | Token | Resolves to | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `component` | button.radius = {radius.control} | `2px` |  |
| `semantic` | radius.control = {radius.md} | `2px` |  |
| `global` | radius.md = 2px | `2px` | **overridden here** |

The highlighted row is the override. Note where it is: `radius.md`, in the
_global_ tier. The seller brand did not touch `button.radius` at all. It changed
a raw value two levels down, and the change arrived at the button through the alias chain. That is
the three-tier design paying for itself.

> **🟡 Watch out — This is also why the chain reaches things you did not think about**
>
> `input.radius` and `checkbox.radius` also point at
> `radius.control` (well, `radius.control-sm` for the checkbox). So the
> seller override reaches them too, automatically. That is usually exactly what you want — and it
> is exactly why you should override at the lowest tier that expresses your intent, not the
> highest one you can reach.

## Brands: the override-only rule

A brand is a folder with one file. The `marketplace` brand is the default and overrides
nothing at all, so its file is literally empty:

**brands/marketplace/tokens.json  [You write this]**

```json
{}
```

The `seller` brand overrides exactly three values:

**brands/seller/tokens.json  [You write this]**

```json
{
  "color": {
    "primary": { "$value": "{color.green.600}" },
    "primary-hover": { "$value": "{color.green.700}" }
  },
  "radius": {
    "md": { "$value": "2px" }
  }
}

```

> **🔴 Important — An overlay may only override. Never add.**
>
> If `brands/seller/tokens.json` introduced a path that does not exist in the base
> token set, that is an error — not a merge. The reason is structural: if brands could add tokens,
> a component contract could reference a token that exists for one brand and not another, and
> there would be no such thing as "one component set that serves every brand". Every brand must
> end up with an identical set of paths, which `validateBrandParity()` checks
> explicitly.
>
> **Brands are skins, never forks.** This rule is what that slogan cashes out to.

Watch the corner radius as well as the colour. The colour comes from a semantic override
(`color.primary`); the radius comes from a global one (`radius.md`) that has
to travel two hops. Both arrive through the same mechanism.

> **🔵 Rule — Why the PaymentButton does not change colour**
>
> `PaymentButton` is an extension that pins its background to `{color.text}`
> and its foreground to `{color.background}` — neither of which any brand overrides. It
> is deliberately brand-independent: a checkout call-to-action that should look identical
> everywhere. Extensions are covered in [chapter 05](05-contracts.md).

## The dependents closure

Here is the part that trips people up. The seller brand overrides three tokens. Its CSS block
contains twelve declarations:

**styles/tokens.css — real output  [girih writes this]**

```css
@layer girih.tokens, girih.components;

@layer girih.tokens {
  [data-brand="seller"] {
    --ds-radius-md: 2px;                                        /* overridden */
    --ds-color-primary: var(--ds-color-green-600);              /* overridden */
    --ds-color-primary-hover: var(--ds-color-green-700);        /* overridden */
    --ds-radius-control: var(--ds-radius-md);                   /* dependent */
    --ds-badge-primary-background: var(--ds-color-primary);     /* dependent */
    --ds-button-primary-background: var(--ds-color-primary);    /* dependent */
    --ds-button-primary-background-hover: var(--ds-color-primary-hover);
    --ds-button-radius: var(--ds-radius-control);               /* dependent */
    --ds-checkbox-background-checked: var(--ds-color-primary);  /* dependent */
    --ds-checkbox-border-hover: var(--ds-color-primary);        /* dependent */
    --ds-input-border-focus: var(--ds-color-primary);           /* dependent */
    --ds-input-radius: var(--ds-radius-control);                /* dependent */
  }
}
```

> **🟡 Watch out — Why the output is wrapped in @layer**
>
> Everything girih emits lands in `@layer girih.tokens` or
> `@layer girih.components`. Unlayered CSS beats layered CSS regardless of
> specificity, so _your_ stylesheet always wins — overriding a generated component
> needs no `!important` and no specificity arms race.
>
> The order statement appears in both stylesheets, not just one. The earliest
> `@layer` declaration establishes precedence, and a consumer may import
> `components.css` first; repeating an identical statement is harmless, so this
> is correct whichever order they load in.

The nine extra declarations are the **dependents closure**: every token that transitively
references an overridden one. They are there because of a specific property of CSS custom
properties that is easy to state and easy to forget.

> **🟡 Watch out — Custom properties are computed where they are declared**
>
> Suppose the emitter had written only the three overrides into the seller block, leaving
> `--ds-button-radius: var(--ds-radius-control)` in `:root`. Inside a
> `[data-brand="seller"]` element, what is `--ds-button-radius`?
>
> It is `8px`. The declaration lives in `:root`, so it was computed against
> `:root`'s `--ds-radius-control`, which resolves to `:root`'s
> `--ds-radius-md` — the un-overridden `8px`. The brand's `2px`
> is simply never consulted. Colour would appear to work (a direct reference) while radius
> silently would not (a two-hop reference), which is the worst possible failure mode: partial.
>
> Re-declaring the chain inside the scope fixes it, because now the whole chain is computed there.
> That is `dependentsClosure()` in
> `packages/girih-generator-css/src/generate.ts`, and it is about twenty lines of
> reverse-graph walk.

## Which declaration wins

That is a lot of words for something you can just try. Turn the closure off and watch the
resolved value change — and note that colour would still appear to work, because
`color.primary` is a direct reference while radius needs two hops. Partial failure is
the whole danger.

> **▶ Which declaration wins?** — interactive
>
> Why the dependents closure is not optional. Open [the interactive version](../04-tokens.html) in a browser to use it.

<details>
<summary><b>The default brand gets a scoped block too — and that is not redundant</b></summary>

Look at the real output and you will find both `:root` _and_
`[data-brand="marketplace"]`, even though marketplace is the default and overrides
nothing. Why emit a block for a brand with no overrides?

Because of nesting. Consider a seller-branded page containing a marketplace-branded widget:
``. Without a
marketplace block, the inner div inherits the seller values — the outer scope's declarations are
still in effect and nothing resets them. So the default brand's block re-declares the closure of
every token that _any_ brand overrides, which restores the base values inside that scope.

This is the kind of detail that only shows up in a real product, usually as a bug report about
one widget on one page looking wrong.

</details>

## What girih checks

| Check | Code | Catches |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unknown reference | `GIRIH2030` | A `{typo}` — with "did you mean" suggestions from the real token set |
| Circular reference | `GIRIH2031` | A → B → A, reported with the full chain, once per cycle |
| Tier direction | `GIRIH2040`–`GIRIH2042` | A reference pointing upward through the tiers |
| Brand parity | `GIRIH2020`–`GIRIH2021` | One brand having a token another lacks |
| Overlay adds a path | `GIRIH2010`–`GIRIH2011` | A brand trying to introduce a new token |
| Unclassifiable file | `GIRIH2004` | A token file whose tier cannot be inferred from its name |
| CSS var collision | `GIRIH3003` | Two token paths mapping to the same custom property name |
| Unflattenable value | `GIRIH3002` | A composite value no CSS transform could serialize |

> **🟡 Watch out — The collision check is subtler than it looks**
>
> `color.primary.hover` and `color.primary-hover` are different token paths.
> Both become `--ds-color-primary-hover`, because the name transform joins segments
> with a hyphen and lowercases. In CSS that is a silent last-one-wins. girih makes it
> `GIRIH3003`, a hard error — one of those bugs that would otherwise cost an afternoon.

---

## Authoring rules

Practical guidance, in rough order of how often it matters:

1. **Name the tier in the filename.** `global*.tokens.json`,  `semantic*.tokens.json`, or under `tokens/components/`. Otherwise you get  a warning and a possibly wrong tier.
2. **Override at the lowest tier that expresses your intent.** Overriding  `radius.md` says "this brand is squarer". Overriding  `button.radius` says "this brand's buttons are squarer, and I accept that inputs and  checkboxes will not match". Both are legitimate; only one is usually meant.
3. **Keep names lowercase and kebab-case.** They become CSS custom property names.  Mixed case invites the collision above.
4. **Declare `$type` on the group, not per token.** Less repetition and it  inherits correctly.
5. **Do not create a semantic token with one consumer.** If exactly one component uses  it, it is a component token wearing a disguise, and the indirection costs a debugging hop.
6. **Run `girih check` before you commit.** It prints the resolved value of  every token for a chosen brand — `--brand seller` — which is faster than reasoning  about the chain in your head.

**[Terminal]**

```
$ pnpm exec girih check --brand seller

TOKEN                     TIER       TYPE       RESOLVED (seller)
button.radius             component  dimension  2px
button.primary.background component  color      #16A34A
radius.control            semantic   dimension  2px
radius.md                 global     dimension  2px
…

6 component contracts: Badge, Button, Card, Checkbox, Dialog, Input
1 extension: PaymentButton → Button
110 tokens (31 global, 25 semantic, 54 component) · 2 brands: marketplace (default), seller (3 overrides)
```

Tokens are the hard half. [Chapter 05](05-contracts.md) is about the other half:
turning a contract into a component that uses them.
